j.learned_fact: "The right side is hot" — one tap gives cold water, the other hot. Note: by standard plumbing convention hot is on the LEFT and cold on the right, so the story teaches the reverse as a rule.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (turning a handle changes water temperature)
j.notes: Pleasant and age-appropriate, but the only "fact" (right tap = hot) contradicts normal plumbing convention, and the "shy little ghost" simile is confusing for bubbles.

j.learned_fact: Hitting a drum hard makes a very loud sound; hitting it gently makes a quiet sound.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (force → volume) and adjusts
j.notes: Two lines are odd or meaningless for a 4-year-old: "Do it soft like clay" and "Soft hits serve the drum better than hard ones" (a drum isn't harmed by hard hits). The lesson is thin and the story ends abruptly.

j.learned_fact: A shape with four sides (a square/rectangle window) differs from one with three sides (a triangle); matching shapes look alike.
j.thinking_skill: compares two shapes by counting sides and fixes the mismatch
j.notes: Window count is muddled (two windows become "both windows" plus "his other window"), and the chalk-on-paper/ground setting flips; one stray tense slip ("He would invite her to sit down"). Shape words "square"/"triangle" are never named, weakening the lesson.

j.learned_fact: A string looped over a rod is a pulley: pulling one side down makes the other side go up. The story's later physics (brush flying "across", paint flung by pulling harder) is muddled and not how a pulley works.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (pull down here, other side rises)
j.notes: The mechanics fall apart after the clear opening demonstration — brushes "dance" and fling paint in ways a string-and-rod pulley couldn't, so the science lesson blurs. Words like "easel", "looped", "machine" plus multi-clause sentences sit slightly above a just-5-year-old reader.

j.learned_fact: Hot things from the oven must cool before you touch them; baking follows a sequence (mix, bake, wait, cool).
j.thinking_skill: follows a sequence and waits for a cause (cooling) before acting
j.notes: The safety/sequence lesson is safely handled but the story is flat—Stella mostly obeys and waits, with no problem of her own; the "ripe strawberry" feels like a bolted-on vocabulary word.

j.learned_fact: A fair-sharing rule (each person gets five pushes, then the next goes) lets everyone have a turn; nothing factual beyond counting to five.
j.thinking_skill: reads a rule and applies it to his own turn
j.notes: The moral is stated outright in the closing paragraph rather than shown, and the counting of five pushes is a thin lesson for a 7-year-old. Logic is slightly odd: Anthony seems to push himself while on the swing, and Maya ignoring him goes unaddressed.

j.learned_fact: Intended: "one cup isn't always the same thing when mixing different ingredients" — but this is muddled/false as stated. Two cups of flour naturally occupy more space than one cup of milk; the story's "discovery" compares unequal amounts and is not a real measurement insight. Also, scooping an overflowing cup is bad measuring practice, presented uncorrected.
j.thinking_skill: notices a difference and asks why (observation, not valid inference)
j.notes: The central "lesson" is logically broken: he compares two cups of flour with one cup of milk and concludes something about equal measures. Grandma also never corrects the overflowing scoop or the non-measuring cabinet cup, so a young reader may absorb wrong ideas about measuring.

j.learned_fact: Rice is a staple in Japan because it grows well in wet, flooded paddy fields — geography shapes diet. (Accurate, though simplified.)
j.thinking_skill: sorts three texts by author's purpose and cites evidence for each
j.notes: It's a media-literacy worksheet wearing a story costume: no conflict, no stakes, nothing happens but a girl making a chart at a table. The "learning" is asserted ("she was starting to see") rather than dramatized.

j.learned_fact: Mixing blue and yellow makes green, and the proportion of each changes the shade — more yellow gives a yellower green, more blue a bluer green. Accurate for pigment/dye mixing.
j.thinking_skill: varies one quantity while holding the other constant and generalizes the pattern
j.notes: The takeaway (proportion affects shade) is a thin, fairly obvious lesson, and the ending purple is unexplained since only blue and yellow are ever used. Prose is flat and summary-like ("She discovered that..."), with little dialogue or sensory life; the setup also promises to explain "why colors change" but never does.

j.learned_fact: Rome endured partly by absorbing and adapting the laws, gods and ideas of conquered peoples rather than forcing uniformity — broadly accurate, though simplified (Rome did impose much and persecuted some cults).
j.thinking_skill: replaces one explanation with a better one and transfers it by analogy
j.notes: The history content is a single tidy monologue that Marcus praises as "brilliant," which flattens the dialogue; the social plot resolves with no real obstacle or conflict.

j.learned_fact: Gas contracts when cooled and expands when warmed because particles move more slowly/take less space when cold — accurate, though "atoms packed tighter" is loosely worded (same amount of air, volume shrinks).
j.thinking_skill: repeats a test to confirm a pattern and infers an unseen cause
j.notes: Solid inquiry arc, but slightly below a 6th-grader's conceptual ceiling (no mention of pressure or controls), and the odd phrase "The pattern was narrow in its consistency" is clumsy; the mom's "That's exactly right" resolves things too easily.

j.learned_fact: Activated charcoal is used as a layer in terrariums to help filter; but the core science is muddled/false — sealed terrarium plants don't "compete for limited CO2" in a way that kills them, and mold using up oxygen is presented as the main collapse mechanism, which is a distortion; plants also produce oxygen and consume CO2 during photosynthesis (true).
j.thinking_skill: notices an anomaly in a claim and researches an explanation
j.notes: The central science is delivered as an encyclopedia paragraph and is partly inaccurate; Raphael never tests anything, he just reads and buys one fewer plant. Vocabulary ("earnest pencil," "I'm trying to express the right balance") is stilted, and the theme is too young and the conflict too slight for a 12-year-old.

j.learned_fact: Base rates depend on the reference class: a 1-in-5 overall success rate doesn't apply to a subgroup (club players had 7 of 8 make the team). Internally inconsistent though—predicting 9 of 12 would make it contradicts the 1-in-5 rate she says she used.
j.thinking_skill: revises a prediction by narrowing the reference class after a failed forecast
j.notes: The central math is inconsistent (applying a 1-in-5 rate yet predicting 9 of 12 succeed), which undercuts the very lesson; the insight is delivered mostly through Ms. Chen's explanatory speech, and the sentence "she should have been subject to what the actual data showed" is garbled. Reads a bit young and thin for 9th grade.

j.learned_fact: That traits like tongue-rolling and earlobe attachment are classic inheritance examples — but the central "lesson" is wrong: a straight-haired sibling of a curly-haired child with one curly and one straight parent is perfectly ordinary Mendelian inheritance (heterozygous parent), not evidence that the gene is "not expressed yet." Hair texture is also polygenic with incomplete dominance, not simple dominant/recessive.
j.thinking_skill: forms a hypothesis from data, then revises it after a prompting question
j.notes: Prose and inquiry arc suit 9th grade, but the genetics payoff is scientifically wrong — the obvious Punnett-square answer (heterozygous curly parent) is never mentioned, so the reader ends up with a misconception dressed as insight.

j.learned_fact: Debugging tactic: insert a print statement before a request to see the actual values being sent; also that latitude/longitude order matters and latitude is the vertical axis. Muddled by the line "she'd reversed the decimal places," which is not the same bug, and "the code itself had been fine the whole time," which contradicts the fix she made.
j.thinking_skill: forms a hypothesis and tests it by instrumenting the program, then verifies with new cases
j.notes: Internal contradictions undercut the lesson: "reversed the decimal places" doesn't describe a swapped lat/long, and claiming "the code was fine the whole time" denies the edit she just made. The Peru moment builds suspense that resolves into nothing, and the closing paragraph turns abstract and preachy.

j.learned_fact: Price can act as a signal of quality ("Price wasn't just a number; it was information"), and revenue is not profit — materials and gas costs must be subtracted.
j.thinking_skill: revises a hypothesis (low price = more sales) after observing contrary market evidence
j.notes: Vocabulary, sentence length and conceptual load sit in the middle-school range, well below an 11th-grade target; the economics stays at the level of a single aphorism (price signalling) without the market or opportunity-cost nuance a 17-year-old could handle. Max's "evidence" — items sitting in strangers' carts — is not actually observable, which weakens the reasoning he models.

j.learned_fact: Aquifers recharge much more slowly than water is pumped out; a model's output is only as good as its input assumptions (here recharge 12,000 gal/day vs 85,000 gal/day consumption).
j.thinking_skill: tests variables one at a time and traces a discrepancy to an unchecked assumption
j.notes: The epistemology lesson is stated repeatedly in narrator's voice ("evidence... didn't prove what you wanted", "That was what the math showed") rather than dramatized; Marcus is a frictionless foil who simply concedes, so there is no real conflict. Serviceable for 11th grade but slightly under-pitched in stakes and prose ambition.

j.learned_fact: Ambiguous behaviour (phone-checking) underdetermines its cause; confirmation bias means arranging evidence to fit a preferred story rather than testing alternative explanations.
j.thinking_skill: recognizes his own confirmation bias and that evidence admits multiple explanations
j.notes: The final paragraph over-explains the lesson and mirrors the unreliable-narrator motif a bit too neatly; the insight is handed to Maxime by Sophie's confession rather than earned by his own testing.

j.learned_fact: Creative Commons repositories let artists share images for reuse with attribution — though the story's claim that view/download counts "accrue measurable value" tracked by a design account's analytics is vague and not accurate as described.
j.thinking_skill: weighs two competing values (impact vs. attribution) without resolving
j.notes: The central mechanism (analytics revealing "uncompensated attention") is hand-waved and technically muddled, so the ethical dilemma floats on abstraction rather than concrete stakes; nothing actually happens and the ambiguity reads as authorial evasion rather than earned irresolution. Prose is essayistic and static.

j.learned_fact: The concept of externalities — costs of a transaction that don't appear on a balance sheet and are borne by people outside it; also algorithmic scheduling minimizing labor costs. Accurate, though the claim that automation forces wages lower is asserted rather than demonstrated.
j.thinking_skill: holds two conflicting evaluations of one system without collapsing them (dialectical reasoning)
j.notes: Almost entirely interior essayizing: the "story" is a girl sitting still while the narration explains labor economics, with the repeated forced word "liable" betraying a vocabulary checklist. The Thai-food girl is a prop rather than a character, and the thesis is stated outright in the final paragraphs instead of being earned by event.

j.learned_fact: Notes that capture your own thinking and context (a teacher's joke) can cue recall better than tidy color-coded notes — a rough gesture at encoding/context-dependent memory, asserted anecdotally rather than established.
j.thinking_skill: generalizes from a single personal experience while explicitly flagging the weakness of that evidence
j.notes: Voice is lively and the epistemic humility ("I have no credentials") is a nice touch, but the stakes and subject matter (first-day-of-junior-year note-taking) sit well below a 12th-grade reader; also an internal slip — "ten-year-old Isla" for notes made last August. Nothing is tested or challenged; the insight is asserted, then affirmed.
